pedagogy.summary: This is a young child's first orientation to the 'big picture' of space: that Earth is one of several planets, that the Sun together with the planets going around it is called the solar system, and that space is the vast region beyond Earth's sky where these things are. At 5–7 the goal is orienting language and a rough mental map, not mechanism — children should be able to say Earth is a planet, use 'solar system' to mean the Sun and its planets, and grasp that space is 'up there', enormously far and mostly empty. The most important conceptual move is decentring: helping children see Earth as one planet among others (not the whole of everything, and not fundamentally different from the other planets), and distinguishing planets (which orbit the Sun and don't make their own light) from the Sun/stars. Because scale is unimaginable and unobservable at this age, teaching leans on models, zoom-out imagery and playful orbiting role-play rather than numbers, and keeps 'space starts high above us, beyond the sky' as the accessible boundary idea.
bestPractices: Build the picture by zooming OUT from the familiar: start on Earth (a place they know), pull back to Earth-as-a-ball-in-space, then to the Sun with planets going round, naming 'solar system' as the whole group
Use 'orbit / goes around' through embodied play: children walk in circles around a 'Sun' to feel that planets travel around it, so 'the Sun and the planets that go around it' is acted, not just told
Explicitly decentre Earth: state and revisit that Earth IS a planet, one of several, so children don't treat it as separate from or bigger than 'the planets'
Keep 'space' concrete as a boundary idea — 'the huge area beyond Earth's sky, where the Sun, Moon, planets and stars are' — and that it is mostly empty and very far away
Distinguish planet from star simply: planets go around the Sun and do not make their own light; the Sun (a star) gives light — foreshadowing later topics without overloading
keyRepresentations: A zoom-out sequence: Earth's ground → Earth as a ball → the Sun with planets orbiting (the canonical orienting image)
A simple Sun-in-the-middle diagram with planets on their paths, 'solar system' labelling the whole
Embodied orbit model (children as planets walking around a central 'Sun')
A picture contrasting 'on Earth / in the sky / out in space' to fix where space is
commonMisconceptions: Earth is not a planet / Earth is separate from or bigger than 'the planets' (Earth is one planet among several)
The Sun is a planet, or planets and stars are the same kind of thing (planets orbit the Sun and don't make their own light)
Space 'starts' just above the rooftops / the sky and space are the same nearby thing (space is enormously far beyond the sky)
The solar system IS the whole universe / everything (it is just our Sun and its planets — a tiny part of a much bigger universe; formalised later)
The Sun goes around the Earth (leave cause aside, but avoid stories that entrench an Earth-centred picture)

learn.summary: First orientation for 5–7 year olds to the 'big picture' of space: Earth is one planet among several, the Sun together with the planets going around it is called the solar system, and space is the vast, mostly empty area far beyond Earth's sky. The goal at this age is orienting vocabulary and a rough mental map, not mechanism. The key conceptual move is decentring — helping children see Earth as one planet among others, not the whole of everything and not fundamentally different from the other planets — and distinguishing planets (which orbit the Sun and don't make their own light) from the Sun/stars. Because scale is unimaginable and unobservable at this age, teaching leans on zoom-out imagery, simple diagrams and playful orbiting role-play rather than numbers.

activities.title: Zoom out from a familiar place into space
feedback: When a child treats Earth as separate from or bigger than 'the planets', replay/retrace the zoom-out so they watch Earth 'become' one ball among several circling the Sun
If a child says space starts just above the rooftops, use the lift-the-flap/point-up-past-the-clouds step to show space is far beyond the sky
Confirm correct naming warmly: 'Yes — Earth is a planet, and all the planets going round the Sun are our solar system'
activities.rationale: Building the picture by zooming OUT from the familiar (ground → Earth-as-a-ball → Sun-with-planets) is intended to let children assemble the nested picture and attach the words 'planet', 'solar system' and 'space' to each part. Tap/reveal naming targets orienting vocabulary rather than mechanism, which is appropriate for this age. The cited sources ground the solar-system content and the known need to decentre Earth, not the effectiveness of the zoom-out method itself. Proposed activity, not an empirically validated intervention.
sourceClaims: The solar system consists of the sun and a collection of objects, including planets, that are held in orbit around the sun — the foundational structure young children are being oriented to (formalised as ESS1.B in later grades).

Young children commonly fail to classify Earth as a planet and treat 'space' as beginning just above the ground; decentring Earth and clarifying the size/emptiness of space are known early-astronomy teaching needs.
learnerActions: Start on a familiar Earth scene — for example a park under a blue sky — then 'zoom out' in stages (on screen with a tap/button, or using a sequence of pictures/paper cards you reveal one at a time)
Watch the ground curve away until the child's whole world is just a blue-and-green ball floating in black
Zoom out again so that ball slides into place as one of several planets looping around a bright Sun, with the whole group labelled 'our solar system'

Name each part as you touch it: tap/point to Earth → 'Earth is a planet — one of several going around the Sun'; the Sun → 'the Sun gives light; the planets go around it'; the black between planets → 'space — the huge, mostly empty area far beyond our sky'
Open a lift-the-flap (or turn a card) answering 'where does space start?' by pointing up past the clouds, far above the sky (point toward the represented scene, not toward the real Sun)
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing their own Earth shrink to one ball among several is intended to help children feel that Earth is a planet like the others, not the whole world, and that space is enormously far beyond the everyday sky.

activities.title: Walk the orbit: become a planet going around the Sun
feedback: If a child says the Sun goes around too, pause the game: the Sun stays in the middle while the planets travel round it
If a child lists the Sun among the planets, remind them the Sun is the star in the middle that gives light; the planets circle it and don't make their own light
activities.rationale: Embodied orbit role-play lets children act out 'goes around / orbits' rather than only being told it, supporting the solar-system idea without introducing orbital physics that is well beyond this age. The cited NGSS claim grounds the solar-system content being acted out (the Sun with objects orbiting it), not the effectiveness of role-play as a method. Proposed activity, not an empirically validated intervention.
sourceClaims: The solar system consists of the sun and a collection of objects, including planets, that are held in orbit around the sun — the foundational structure young children are being oriented to (formalised as ESS1.B in later grades).
learnerActions: Set up a central 'Sun' (a child, a lamp, or a marked spot) and have children walk in circles around it to act out 'the planets travel around the Sun'
Say the sentence as they move: 'the Sun stays in the middle while the planets go around it'
Point out that the Sun gives light while the planets do not make their own light — they are lit up by the Sun
Pause to 'find Earth' among the moving planets and confirm Earth is one of the ones going around
activities.intendedInsight: Acting out orbiting is intended to make 'the Sun and the planets that go around it' something children feel in their bodies, reinforcing the meaning of 'solar system' and that the Sun sits in the middle with planets circling it.

activities.title: Watch the planets orbit the Sun
feedback: Keep it purely illustrative: if a child asks why, acknowledge the question but keep the focus on naming and noticing rather than mechanism
Praise correctly finding Earth among the planets and naming the whole group as the solar system
activities.rationale: A watch-and-name animation is intended to support the orbit vocabulary introduced in the zoom-out and role-play activities. It is a support rather than the primary teaching step, which is naming/orienting. The cited source grounds the solar-system content named here, not the animation's effectiveness; proposed activity, not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: The solar system consists of the sun and a collection of objects, including planets, that are held in orbit around the sun — the foundational structure young children are being oriented to (formalised as ESS1.B in later grades).
learnerActions: Press play on a simple Sun-with-orbiting-planets animation (or watch the walking-orbit game) and watch the planets circle the Sun
Tap/point to a planet to hear or say its name
Respond to a gentle 'find Earth' prompt and confirm Earth is one of the orbiting planets
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing 'going around the Sun' in motion is intended to make the orbit idea concrete and reinforce that Earth is one of several planets circling the Sun.

activities.title: Check: where things are and what counts as our solar system
feedback: Full grasp: states Earth is one of the planets orbiting the Sun, names the group as the solar system, and distinguishes the planets from the central Sun-star and from the far-off night stars
Partial: says Earth is a planet but cannot connect it to the Sun or use 'solar system', or is unsure whether the Sun and distant stars belong — revisit the zoom-out and orbit steps
Gap: says Earth is not a planet, or calls the Sun a planet — use the zoom-out model so Earth is seen as one ball circling the Sun
If a child folds the twinkly night stars into our solar system, explain other stars are enormously far away, far beyond the solar system, and save the full scale idea for later
activities.rationale: Picture matching, sorting and a why-tier diagnostic can check whether orienting vocabulary has taken hold, including the decentring move. The spoken two-tier 'why' is a diagnostic that elicits the child's own reasoning; the two framings it offers are prompts to surface a possible misconception, not a factual answer key — 'Earth is something different and special that isn't really a planet' is the error being probed, not a valid option. Matching and sorting primarily confirm naming and may also reinforce it through retrieval, but recognition alone does not by itself elicit the independent spoken explanation the 'why' tier draws out. Because these checks mainly confirm rather than introduce the concept, they follow the zoom-out and role-play activities.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly fail to classify Earth as a planet and treat 'space' as beginning just above the ground; decentring Earth and clarifying the size/emptiness of space are known early-astronomy teaching needs.
learnerActions: Match each word to its picture: planet / Sun / space

Sort pictures into 'on Earth / in the sky (e.g. clouds, birds, aeroplanes) / out in space (e.g. the Sun, Moon, planets, stars)', explaining that the Sun, Moon and stars can be seen in our sky but are really far away out in space
Pick 'which of these is our solar system?' from simple picture options showing the Sun with its planets
Answer and explain: 'Is Earth a planet, the same kind of thing as the other planets — or is Earth something different and special that isn't really a planet at all? Tell me which, and WHY'
activities.intendedInsight: Children can show they recognise Earth as a planet, name the solar system and place where space is — and the 'why' reveals whether they genuinely see Earth as one member of the solar system or are just reciting the word 'planet'. The 'something different and special' option is the misconception being probed, not a correct answer.

constraints: At 5–7 the goal is orienting language and a rough mental map, not mechanism: children should be able to say Earth is a planet, use 'solar system' for the Sun and its planets, and grasp that space is 'up there', very far and mostly empty. Do not introduce orbital dynamics, numbers or scale figures.
Explicitly and repeatedly decentre Earth: state that Earth IS a planet, one of several, so children don't treat it as separate from or bigger than 'the planets'.
Keep 'space' concrete as a boundary idea — the huge area beyond Earth's sky where the Sun, Moon, planets and stars are — and note it is mostly empty and very far away.
Distinguish planet from star simply: planets go around the Sun and do not make their own light; the Sun (a star) gives light. Avoid overloading with more than this.
The solar system is just our Sun and its planets — a tiny part of a much bigger universe. Do not equate it with the whole universe; that distinction is formalised later.

Leave the cause of day/night and Sun/Earth motion aside, but avoid stories that entrench a Sun-going-around-the-Earth, Earth-centred picture. Model the Sun as sitting in the middle with planets circling it, framed relationally rather than claiming the Sun is absolutely motionless.
The animation and orbit game are illustrative supports, not physics simulations; do not treat them as mechanistic explanations.
The recognition/matching check confirms naming (and may reinforce it) but does not by itself elicit the independent explanation that the spoken 'why' prompt draws out — keep both.

A manipulable 3D navigable model is not needed at this age: the learning is naming and rough orientation, and free-navigation can add handling cost without helping children attach the words. Offer it only if it clearly supports naming; this is a narrow affordance observation, not a claim that 3D adds nothing to learning in general.
When checking where space is, observe the represented scene and point up past the clouds; do not ask children to look at or toward the real Sun, or to hold any material up toward it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources were marked unverified in the source row (the England National Curriculum placement note and the misconceptions/decentring claim); treat their specific attributions cautiously. The NGSS ESS1.B structural claim was marked verified.

The source row notes KS1 (ages 5–7) has no statutory UK space unit and this early orientation is anchored on US grade-band expectations; the 5–7 age target is therefore a pedagogical choice rather than a national-curriculum requirement.

Original non-preferred entries (open conversation; manipulable 3D model) were rated 'poor' on catalog-fit grounds. Their genuine limits are captured in constraints as narrowly scoped affordance notes, not as universal laws about the medium.
The source claim that distant night stars are 'enormously far beyond the solar system' is scientifically sound and preserved; keep scale strictly qualitative at this age.
The 'Sun stays in the middle' model is the source's age-appropriate simplification; framed relationally it is faithful, but note the Sun is not literally motionless if an older learner probes.

The two-tier diagnostic in the final check deliberately presents the 'Earth is something different and special' misconception as a framing to surface the child's reasoning; it is a probe, not a correct option, and should never be scored as a valid answer.

probeDeeper: If you flew far out into space and looked back, what would Earth look like?
What is at the centre of the solar system, holding all the planets in their paths?
Are the twinkly stars we see at night part of our solar system, or much, much further away?
What do we mean by the word 'space'?
assess.correctAnswer: Earth IS a planet — one of the planets that orbit the Sun. Our Sun together with the group of planets going round it is called the solar system. Earth feels special because we live on it, but it is the same KIND of thing as the other planets: a big ball travelling around the Sun.

errorPatterns.pattern: Earth isn't a planet — it's the ground we live on, or the centre of everything ('planets are those other things out in space')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a zoom-out model: ground → Earth as a whole ball → Earth as one of several balls circling the Sun; let the child watch Earth 'become' a planet.
errorPatterns.distractor: Earth is different — it's the ground we live on, not a planet like the others.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets Earth apart from 'the planets' and treats it as the fixed ground rather than an orbiting ball

errorPatterns.pattern: the Sun is one of the planets ('the Sun goes round with the rest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the Sun as the star at the centre that the planets orbit around; it stays put while the planets travel round it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun is one of the planets in the solar system.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child lists the Sun among the planets or says the Sun orbits too

errorPatterns.pattern: the twinkly night stars are part of our solar system ('they're just past our sky')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain other stars are enormously far away, far beyond the solar system; save the full scale idea for later topics.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child folds the distant stars into the solar system

responseLevels.gap: Says Earth is not a planet, or calls the Sun a planet; no sense of Earth as one ball orbiting the Sun.
responseLevels.full: States Earth is one of the planets orbiting the Sun, names the group as the solar system, and distinguishes the planets from the central Sun-star and from the far-off night stars.
responseLevels.partial: Says Earth is a planet but cannot connect it to the Sun or use the term 'solar system', or is unsure whether the Sun and distant stars belong to it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is the Earth a planet, the same kind of thing as the other planets in space — or is Earth something different and special that isn't really a planet at all? Tell me which, and WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who still experiences Earth as the flat, central ground rather than one ball among many says Earth is different and special. A child who has decentred says Earth is a planet like the others and can place it as orbiting the Sun. The 'why' tier separates reciting the word 'planet' from genuinely seeing Earth as one member of the solar system.

sources.claim: England's National Curriculum places Earth and space (Sun at the centre of the solar system, Earth as a planet) at Year 5; at KS1 (ages 5–7) there is no statutory space unit, so this early solar-system orientation is anchored on US grade-band expectations and taught informally through observation and models.
